questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was important for me that I came to a country in which people would speak English as their first language. I chose Canada for this exact reason, and I have definitely benefited from being around native English speakers every day.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I honestly don't know how my exchange year could have been better. I have had the time of my life, met great people and have had classes with engaging professors and interesting topics. Overall, my study abroad experience has been fantastic and very insightful.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy. The exchange office at SFU has been very helpful, so I haven't been in a situation where I couldn't find the information that I needed. People around me have also been very helpful. Secondly, we were added to a group on Canvas called SFU Exchange 101, wherein we could find plenty of information about being and exchange student at SFU and about the university in general.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Well, as I have written above, the exchange office has been a great source of help. And then because I lived in residence, the Residence and Housing office helped a lot as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I could choose from 5 different places on campus, which I had done almost half a year before going. I ended up living in one of the Towers in which I had my own room but shared washrooms with 24 other people. It's primarily for first years, so be prepared to live with people that are way younger than yourself. It didn't affect me that much, but it's important to keep it in my mind.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I was on the meal plan (it's mandatory if you live in the North Towers) which meant I got food every day. The dining hall is open 24/7, so I have never had to worry about getting food.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Chose the meal plan! It's the best! They have a variety of foods, and it's just super nice to go in and eat whatever food you want without having to plan it and cook it. I am a vegetarian, and they always served really good vegan food. The food varies from breakfast, lunch and dinner, and after 10 pm it's only a small part of the dining hall that is open, but it's the best when you come home from a night out - the pizza slice and fries hit very well.  
Furthermore, the dining hall has been a great place for me to meet people. I quickly found a group of friends, and we ate lunch and dinner together almost every day for all the time we were there.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I haven't heard of anyone who didn't get housing on campus, so overall, it has been great for all exchange students. Some chose to stay off-campus, but I wouldn't recommend it. The R5 bus goes all the time from Downtown to SFU, but it's so convenient to be on campus and walk back and forth from class to the dining hall or to your residence.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We had to enroll in courses in early July (for reference our semester started in early September), and then once we started here we had a period of 2 weeks in which we could drop and select courses if any spots were available. If spots were available, we could enroll in those courses we wanted.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The exchange office did all the work for us. They enrolled us in the different courses and helped us drop and select new ones.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Because I study something very specific in Denmark, I had none of the prerequisites to get more advanced courses. For example, I could only get psychology 100, even though I have had educational psychology back home. This wasn't enough for me to be able to get any courses in psychology that weren't either 100 or 102. That being said, the course has been very interesting and not too easy. 
I had made a list of 4 courses I wanted that were approved by KU, but when I came here, the courses were either full or I was not able to register for them, because I didn't meet the prerequisites. I ended up having 3 other courses than the ones I had been approved for, but the overall process has been quite easy.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress too much about courses beforehand. Get over here and see how the courses are, and then you can drop and enroll in new courses. If you don't meet the prerequisites, send an email to the professor and explain why you would like to be in that specific class, and maybe they will let you in the class anyways. I know some of my friends did this and it worked for them.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I have only had level 100 courses, but they haven't been a walk in the park at all, even though it has primarily been first-year courses. It has been a good mix of easy and more difficult content.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I have almost only had lectures, meaning I have been sitting in class and listening. I have enjoyed being able to sit in class and listen to professors who are very good at what they do and have a lot of knowledge in their respective areas. 
Furthermore, we have had weekly quizzes and assignments that we sometimes have done in class, so for me, it has been like going to a Danish high school actually. I have enjoyed this method of teaching a lot more than the one I am used to back home in Denmark.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I was enrolled in PSYC100 (Psychology), CMNS110 (Communication), HSCI160 (Global Health) and LING160 (Linguistics). It has been four very different courses, but of course, they are all part of "social science", which is why I have been able to take them. It was very insightful to have courses that have been so different because I feel like I've learned a lot in different areas.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Take courses that you find interesting and make sure the workload is spread out. I only have one course with a final exam, and instead, I have been doing assignments throughout the semester, which have taken a lot of the pressure off.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I have gone out way more than I do back home, so alcohol has been an unexpected cost for me.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The prices are very similar to the ones in Denmark when you add taxes (remember that, I always forget)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I haven't joined any clubs since the hiking club, that I wanted to join, wasn't available this autumn.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
We have access to the gym and some of the facilities like soccer fields. We have been to hockey games and American football games at school.
Secondly, they have drop-in sports, which means you can come and join a volleyball game, or futsal or badminton etc. They have a schedule in which you can see what kinds of drop-in sports are available throughout the week.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go to the official games that the host university has! It's a fun thing to experience. Remember loads of clothes if you go to an American football game in the winter (it's so cold). 
Remember to take academic breaks, and do fun things throughout the week, so you don't get caught up in school so much.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
GO ON HIKES! There are so many amazing hikes in British Columbia, so when the weather allows it, go out and explore the nature! When it's raining, go out and do fun activities in Vancouver, they have a lot of indoor things to do like mini golfing, escape rooms etc. 
I have also gone on longer trips, like weekend trips to Toronto or Banff. I have really enjoyed that as well since the prices for flights aren't too expensive when you fly domestically.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Canadian culture isn't that different from the Danish, or at least Western culture, so I don't feel like it has been a big adjustment in that case. Canadians are very welcoming, so it hasn't been hard to talk with people. The toughest thing for me has definitely been the age difference! Most of the people from my dorm are 18 years, and I turned 24 throughout my stay. 6 years really does a lot, which also meant I have spent a lot of time with other exchange students because we were more alike in terms of age, and because we all had the same mindset toward our stay at SFU.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be friendly and open and speak English all the time, even though you hang out with people that speak Danish too. We have gotten many friends from speaking English in public spaces because people approach you because they understand you. You can quickly become a tight-knitted group if you speak your native language, so I would really recommend speaking English all the time (even though it might be a bit weird in the beginning)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: As I wrote, the age has been a huge difference and then sarcasm. I am used to being ironic or sarcastic in Danish, but I haven't been that as much here. I find it difficult to be so when I speak a foreign language. Sometimes, I have also had trouble getting if someone else was being sarcastic because I can't detect it as well in English as I can in Danish. But it's a small thing that is quite easy to adapt to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Canadians are so nice and polite. They are very friendly and talk with many different people without really knowing them. Many people have shown great interest in hearing about Danish culture and how we do things back home.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Bring hiking shoes 
Speak English all the time
Say yes to all activities that are arranged

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Save up money! You spent a lot of money on trips etc., and you don't wish to sit them out because you can't afford them.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the amazing friendships I have gotten. I have met many people from different parts of the world, which is super beneficial in future situations.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: If you are an introvert and prefer to have some time alone, it can be hard and challenging because you hang out with people all the time. And you don't want to say no to stuff, so you keep pushing yourself a bit more, which can make you super tired some days.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
